items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Selye’s three-stage model of the body’s response to prolonged stress: alarm, resistance and exhaustion”?
items.answer: General adaptation syndrome (GAS)
items.markingKey: General adaptation syndrome (GAS): Selye’s three-stage model of the body’s response to prolonged stress: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Prolonged stress can make people more likely to become ill. Reason (R): In the exhaustion stage of the GAS, the body’s resources are depleted and immune function is weakened. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: This is Selye’s explanation. [1]

items.stem: Describe the general adaptation syndrome.
items.answer: Alarm: the stressor is detected and the sympathetic system and adrenaline produce fight or flight. Resistance: the body adapts and maintains high arousal with cortisol. Exhaustion: with continued stress, resources are depleted and stress-related illness may develop.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each stage [3]

items.stem: In the last year, Mei, from Istanbul, experienced: marriage (50 LCU); being fired at work (47 LCU); change in residence (20 LCU); death of a close family member (63 LCU); change to a different line of work (36 LCU); marital separation (65 LCU). Calculate Mei’s total life change units (LCU).
items.markingKey: 50 + 47 + 20 + 63 + 36 + 65 = 281. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: In the last year, Isla, from Doha, experienced: death of a spouse (100 LCU); son or daughter leaving home (29 LCU); minor violations of the law (11 LCU); change in eating habits (15 LCU). (a) Calculate Isla’s total life change units (LCU). (b) Holmes and Rahe suggested that 300 or more LCU is high risk and 150–299 moderate risk of stress-related illness. State the level of risk.
items.answer: (a) 155 (b) Moderate risk (155 LCU)
items.markingKey: (a) 100 + 29 + 11 + 15 = 155. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 155 LCU → moderate risk [1]

items.stem: In the last year, Ines, from Toronto, experienced: son or daughter leaving home (29 LCU); change in financial state (38 LCU); death of a spouse (100 LCU); outstanding personal achievement (28 LCU). (a) Calculate Ines’s total life change units (LCU). (b) Suggest a physiological measure that could be used alongside the SRRS and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 195 (b) Salivary cortisol or blood pressure, which give objective evidence of the stress response that is not affected by self-report bias.
items.markingKey: (a) 29 + 38 + 100 + 28 = 195. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark measure; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Evaluate Holmes and Rahe’s Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS), including a discussion of practicality.
items.answer: Strength (quantitative data): It gives a single LCU score that can be compared and correlated with illness. Strength (practicality): It is quick and easy to complete and score. Weakness (validity): Some events are ambiguous (for example “change in health”) and it ignores daily hassles and chronic stressors. Weakness (individual differences): Fixed values ignore the meaning of events for each person (for example a wanted divorce may be a relief). Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.answer: Factors such as high workload, lack of control, repetitive machine-paced tasks, long hours and conflict can cause stress; Johansson et al. found repetitive, responsible sawmill work raised adrenaline and illness; Chandola et al. linked work stress to heart disease.

items.stem: Explain one strength and one weakness of physiological measures of stress.
items.answer: Strength: they are objective and not affected by social desirability. Weakness: arousal can be caused by things other than stress (exercise, excitement, caffeine), and equipment may itself be stressful.

items.stem: Describe the procedure of Geer and Maisel (1972).
items.answer: Participants viewed photographs of dead car-crash victims while GSR and heart rate were recorded; one group could press a button to end each photo, one group was warned when photos would appear and how long they would last, and one group had no control or warning.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of physiological measures of stress (such as GSR, heart rate and cortisol). Include at least one point about validity.
items.answer: Strength (objectivity): They provide numerical data that are not affected by participants’ honesty or memory. Strength (reliability): Standardised equipment gives consistent readings that can be repeated. Weakness (ethics): Some measures (such as blood samples) are invasive and may cause discomfort or anxiety. Weakness (validity): Arousal can be caused by excitement or exercise, so high readings do not always mean stress. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Describe the three phases of stress inoculation training.
items.answer: Conceptualisation: the client learns about stress and identifies stressors and thoughts. Skill acquisition and rehearsal: coping skills such as relaxation, positive self-statements and problem-solving are taught and practised. Application and follow-through: skills are used in increasingly stressful real situations with follow-up sessions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each phase [3]

items.stem: Explain how biofeedback can be used to manage stress.
items.answer: Sensors measure a physiological response (for example muscle tension or heart rate) and display it as a sound or graph; the person practises relaxation and learns which strategies reduce the response, until they can control it without the equipment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark feedback; 1 mark learning control [2]

items.stem: Diego, a teacher in Istanbul, suffers from tension headaches and a racing heart before school inspections. Suggest how biofeedback could help Diego.
items.answer: Use EMG sensors on the forehead to show muscle tension; Diego practises relaxation until tension drops, learning to relax without the equipment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark sensors/feedback; 1 mark learned control [2]

items.stem: “Stress inoculation training (SIT) has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including side effects in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (side effects): Unlike drugs, it has no physical side effects or risk of dependence. Strength (long-term effectiveness): It teaches coping skills that can be used with future stressors, so benefits last. Weakness (generalisability): It may suit people who are motivated and able to learn cognitive skills, but not everyone. Weakness (practicality): It requires time, motivation and a trained therapist, so it is costly. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that self-report scales are the best way to measure stress? In your answer, you may refer to reliability, individual differences and validity.
items.answer: Arguments for: The SRRS and hassles scales are quick, cheap and can be given to large samples. They measure the person’s own perception of stress. items.markingKey: 1 mark drug; 1 mark mechanism [2]

items.stem: Noah asked 10 students in Colombo to complete a life events scale (LCU score) and recorded the number of days they were ill in the following six months. Data (LCU score, days of illness) for each participant: (254, 7); (447, 19); (293, 8); (257, 7); (257, 10); (339, 13); (150, 5); (403, 13); (311, 10); (240, 7). (a) Name the type of graph that should be used to display these data and state what would be shown on each axis. (b) Calculate the mean LCU score. Give your answer to one decimal place.
items.answer: (a) A scatter graph, with LCU score on one axis (x-axis) and days of illness on the other (y-axis); each participant is one point. (b) 295.1
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: scatter graph; 1 mark: axes labelled with both co-variables [2] (b) 2951 ÷ 10 = 295.1 [1]

items.stem: Tariq, a teacher in Mexico City, suffers from tension headaches and a racing heart before school inspections. (a) Suggest how biofeedback could help Tariq. (b) Explain why SIT might be better for Tariq in the long term.
items.answer: (a) Use EMG sensors on the forehead to show muscle tension; Tariq practises relaxation until tension drops, learning to relax without the equipment. (b) It teaches coping skills for future inspections and other stressors without side effects or dependence.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark sensors/feedback; 1 mark learned control [2] (b) 1 mark skills; 1 mark no side effects [2]

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Minor, everyday irritations, such as losing keys or traffic, that can add up to cause stress”?
items.answer: Daily hassles
items.markingKey: Daily hassles: minor, everyday irritations, such as losing keys or traffic, that can add up to cause stress. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Daily hassles may be a better predictor of stress than major life events.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Only negative events count as life events on the SRRS.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Research such as Kanner et al. found hassles related strongly to psychological symptoms. (b) Not correct. Positive events such as marriage and holidays also require readjustment and are included.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Outline one weakness of Holmes and Rahe’s Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS) that relates to individual differences.
items.answer: Fixed values ignore the meaning of events for each person (for example a wanted divorce may be a relief).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to individual differences; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Tariq measured heart rate (bpm) during a public-speaking task for employees with or without stress inoculation training. Table: Heart rate during presentation (bpm) — SIT: 86, 90, 84, 86, 93, 86, 89, 106. No training: 94, 95, 112, 95, 97, 97, 99, 98. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The no training condition had a higher mean (98.4) than the SIT condition (90.0), suggesting that stress inoculation training reduces the physiological stress response.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: Kwame asked 9 students in Karachi to complete a life events scale (LCU score) and recorded the number of days they were ill in the following six months. Data (LCU score, days of illness) for each participant: (213, 10); (114, 8); (335, 15); (77, 4); (165, 4); (72, 6); (272, 13); (199, 10); (414, 18). Explain why Kwame cannot conclude that LCU score causes the change in days of illness.
items.answer: A correlation only shows that two variables are related; neither was manipulated, so the direction of cause is unknown and a third variable, such as poor diet or lack of sleep, could affect both.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no manipulation / relationship only; 1 mark: third variable or direction problem explained in context [2]

items.stem: In the last year, Chloe, from Mexico City, experienced: minor violations of the law (11 LCU); change in residence (20 LCU); trouble with boss (23 LCU); change in financial state (38 LCU). (a) Calculate Chloe’s total life change units (LCU). (b) Holmes and Rahe suggested that 300 or more LCU is high risk and 150–299 moderate risk of stress-related illness. State the level of risk.
items.answer: (a) 92 (b) Low risk (92 LCU)
items.markingKey: (a) 11 + 20 + 23 + 38 = 92. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 92 LCU → low risk [1]

items.stem: A study in Doha measured life change units (LCU) and days of illness over the next six months for 10 adults. Data (LCU score, days of illness) for each participant: (153, 9); (145, 7); (166, 11); (324, 15); (182, 9); (432, 16); (268, 15); (249, 14); (234, 12); (127, 5). (a) Name the type of graph that should be used to display these data and state what would be shown on each axis. (b) Calculate the mean LCU score. Give your answer to one decimal place. (c) Calculate the range of the days of illness scores.
items.answer: (a) A scatter graph, with LCU score on one axis (x-axis) and days of illness on the other (y-axis); each participant is one point. (b) 228.0 (c) 11
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: scatter graph; 1 mark: axes labelled with both co-variables [2] (b) 2280 ÷ 10 = 228.0 [1] (c) 16 − 5 = 11 [1]

items.stem: ‘Psychological methods are more effective than medical methods for managing stress.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to practicality and side effects.
items.answer: Arguments for: SIT and biofeedback teach skills that last and have no side effects (Budzynski et al., 1973). Arguments against: Drugs such as benzodiazepines and beta-blockers work quickly and need little effort. Psychological methods take time and motivation. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Holmes and Rahe’s list of 43 life events, each with a value in life change units”?
items.answer: Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS)
items.markingKey: Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS): Holmes and Rahe’s list of 43 life events, each with a value in life change units. [1]

items.stem: Outline one strength of physiological measures of stress (such as GSR, heart rate and cortisol) that relates to reliability.
items.answer: Standardised equipment gives consistent readings that can be repeated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to reliability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Physiological measures of stress (such as GSR, heart rate and cortisol) can be evaluated in terms of ethics. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Some measures (such as blood samples) are invasive and may cause discomfort or anxiety.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to ethics; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A school in Lisbon wants to measure stress in students during exam season. Explain one problem with the physiological measure for this purpose.
items.answer: It is costly and needs equipment or samples; readings may be affected by exercise or caffeine, not just stress.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Mohammed asked 8 students in Mexico City to complete a life events scale (LCU score) and recorded the number of days they were ill in the following six months. Data (LCU score, days of illness) for each participant: (443, 18); (270, 8); (73, 3); (299, 14); (209, 11); (245, 13); (137, 8); (99, 9). (a) Write a non-directional hypothesis for this study. (b) Calculate the mean LCU score. Give your answer to one decimal place. (c) Calculate the range of the days of illness scores.
items.answer: (a) There will be a correlation between life change units in the past year and days of illness in the next six months. (b) 221.9 (c) 15
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correlation (not difference) stated; 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised [2] (b) 1775 ÷ 8 = 221.9 [1] (c) 18 − 3 = 15 [1]

items.stem: Define the term ‘biofeedback’.
items.answer: A technique that gives a person information about a physiological process (such as muscle tension) so they can learn to control it.
items.markingKey: Biofeedback: a technique that gives a person information about a physiological process (such as muscle tension) so they can learn to control it. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the three phases of stress inoculation training. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “SIT aims to prepare people to cope with future stressors as well as current ones.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Conceptualisation: the client learns about stress and identifies stressors and thoughts. Skill acquisition and rehearsal: coping skills such as relaxation, positive self-statements and problem-solving are taught and practised. Application and follow-through: skills are used in increasingly stressful real situations with follow-up sessions. (b) Correct. Like a vaccination, it builds resistance.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each phase [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Stress inoculation training (SIT) can be evaluated in terms of practicality. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: It requires time, motivation and a trained therapist, so it is costly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to practicality; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A company in Santiago compared heart rate (beats per minute) during a stressful presentation for 8 employees who had completed stress inoculation training and 8 who had not. Table: Heart rate during presentation (bpm) — SIT: 74, 80, 86, 85, 86, 91, 79, 88. No training: 103, 86, 90, 111, 108, 91, 104, 99. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: SIT: 83.6; no training: 99.0.
items.markingKey: SIT: 669 ÷ 8 = 83.6; no training: 792 ÷ 8 = 99.0. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: Zara asked 8 students in Lima to complete a life events scale (LCU score) and recorded the number of days they were ill in the following six months. Data (LCU score, days of illness) for each participant: (436, 18); (315, 12); (89, 7); (401, 13); (444, 20); (70, 4); (93, 10); (63, 6). (a) State the type of correlation shown by these data.
